title: Deadly Livestock Virus Found Lurking in Ancient Texts - Nautilus
gist: A University College Dublin-led team extracted ancient virus DNA from the animal-skin parchment pages of medieval European manuscripts, including the roughly 1,000-year-old York Gospels and an early Corpus Christi College Cambridge dictionary, showing historic archives can double as biological specimen repositories.

insights.claim: Medieval parchment manuscripts, made from washed, stretched, and scraped animal skin, are durable enough to preserve viral DNA for centuries, letting researchers extract genetic material from the animals the parchment originally came from.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Establishes library and archive collections as an underused genomic dataset for tracking historical livestock disease evolution, of interest to paleogenomics and biosecurity research.

insights.claim: A team of international researchers led by agricultural scientists at University College Dublin extracted DNA from animal-skin pages of archaic manuscripts across Europe, including the roughly 1,000-year-old York Gospels (previously used in prior DNA studies) and the Corpus Christi College Cambridge manuscript, one of the earliest surviving English dictionaries, finding they were riddled with viruses.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Names specific historical manuscripts and an institution now positioned as a hub for medieval-document paleogenomics research.
